nodes.question: What stays alive when I close a window, disconnect, log out, or restart?
nodes.why_ask: An app window, a network connection, a login session, a running process, and saved state have different lifetimes. Which event actually ended the work?

nodes.question: Why can my computer be busy but make no useful progress?
nodes.why_ask: High CPU usage can mean productive work, spinning, contention, reclaim, interrupt load or stalled progress. Which measurable resource is limiting the task?

nodes.question: Why can one program run out of memory while another still works?
nodes.why_ask: Virtual addresses, physical pages, allocation limits, swapping and out-of-memory policy are different resources and boundaries.

nodes.question: Could a browser, robot, or game console be my whole operating environment?
nodes.why_ask: The experience someone uses can differ radically even when a familiar kernel, embedded runtime or remote machine supplies most system services.

nodes.question: Can a broken component recover without restarting the whole computer?
nodes.why_ask: Fault containment, restart supervision, persistent state and safe recovery are distinct contracts; surviving a crash is not the same as resuming correctly.

nodes.question: Why can an app access a file but not a camera, another app, or a remote service?
nodes.why_ask: Filesystems, process privileges, device mediation and remote authorization enforce different access boundaries; a single notion of 'permission' hides the mechanism.

connections.why: Running arbitrary programs introduces trust and privilege questions
Concurrent programs interact through address spaces and shared state
A restart is often where mistaken persistence assumptions become visible
Alternative architectures can change what 'building an OS' means
Boot and device interaction both depend on the target machine's contracts
What counts as a useful OS depends on why the user wants one
A different user experience may not require a new kernel
A device with trusted programs may need different protection guarantees
What one person can build depends strongly on which components are reused
A session can end while persistent data survives, or remain alive while unsaved data is lost.
CPU occupancy does not imply progress when tasks are contending or spinning.
Virtual isolation does not make physical memory infinite.
A distinct operating experience may be built above a reused kernel.
Recovery must be demonstrated after fault and restart, not inferred from successful initialization.
Resource-specific authorization is not equivalent to a single all-or-nothing kernel boundary.

source_reference_policy: Candidate reference ranges are reading leads indexed by printed book pages, not established Certificates (C). Exact evidentiary citations and conclusions belong in investigation records after reading.
guidance: Speak like a curious human. Start from the user's actual ambition. Ask deceptively simple questions; consider plausible yes / yes-but / no / no-unless branches only when they change what to investigate. Do not substitute an artificial syllabus or technical headings for the question tree. Follow RSM-01.03, RSM-02.08–02.12, RSM-08.10.
previous_tree_note: The earlier abstract OS-01..OS-08 topic-centered tree remains in Git history before this revision; this is a deliberate re-rooting, not a renaming.
next_collaborative_step: Use question-to-chapter navigation for OSTEP as a reference, not ask the user to rediscover general OS knowledge or specify an OS-building purpose.

entries.question: Why is the computer busy even when nothing useful gets done?
entries.context: CPU utilization is not a correctness or progress metric.

entries.question: Why does running out of memory slow everything down or kill one app?
entries.context: Differentiate address-space mappings, reclaim and process quotas.

entries.question: How can two programs use the same memory address without colliding?
entries.context: Numeric addresses acquire meaning through their process mapping.

entries.question: Why can an app read one thing but not a camera, another app or a remote service?
entries.context: Find the responsible authorization mechanism rather than treating permission as universal.

entries.question: Why does plugging in a device sometimes need a driver or cause a freeze?
entries.context: Hardware events, driver code and scheduling interact.

entries.question: Why can a file be lost even though I pressed Save?
entries.context: A successful write may not be a durable commit.

entries.question: What must a computer do to recover safely after a crash?
entries.context: Correct recovery preserves invariants and progress, not merely rebootability.

entries.question: Why can I disconnect from a computer and find my programs still running?
entries.context: A client connection can disappear without ending the server-side process.

entries.question: What is the difference between closing a window, logging out and restarting?
entries.context: Identify which state owner each action destroys.

entries.question: How does a computer get from turning on to running my own code?
entries.context: Identify firmware, loader, privileged runtime and their handoff contracts.

entries.question: Could I make a browser, console or robot into the computer's entire interface?
entries.context: Separate what users experience from what trusted system services supply.

entries.question: What is the smallest useful OS I could build without reinventing everything?
entries.context: Choose the minimal capability set and identify reusable infrastructure.

entries.question: Can several computers behave like one coherent system?
entries.context: Shared experience does not imply shared failure, identity or consistency guarantees.

entries.question: What should happen when software controlling a real device gets stuck?
entries.context: Physical deadlines and safe failure states can matter more than general-purpose throughput.

curiosity_atlas.entry_policy: Entry formulations are discovery surfaces; bridge choices explain consequential differences. They are not separate copies of technical investigations.

navigation_bridges.question: Which part of the system is still making progress?

choices.label: A program is blocked, spinning, or starved
choices.distinguishing_question: Can the kernel still schedule other work, and what is the blocked task waiting for?
choices.why: An unresponsive window can coexist with a healthy scheduler. CPU saturation, sleeping on I/O and starvation require different observations.

choices.label: Devices or memory pressure stall the whole system
choices.technical_title: Page faults, reclaim, interrupt and device paths
choices.distinguishing_question: Is time being spent reclaiming memory, faulting pages, or servicing a device?
choices.why: A fast CPU cannot hide a bottleneck that forces most progress to wait on memory or device completion.

navigation_bridges.question: Which resource or address-space contract failed?

choices.label: Addresses appear identical across processes
choices.distinguishing_question: Do equal virtual addresses resolve to the same physical page or two different mappings?
choices.why: An address is meaningful only relative to its address-space mapping; equality of numeric addresses does not imply aliasing.

choices.label: Memory is exhausted or slow
choices.distinguishing_question: Is failure caused by virtual-space limits, resident-memory pressure, reclaim, or explicit process quotas?
choices.why: Allocated, mapped, committed and resident bytes are not interchangeable. Repeated page faults can dominate elapsed time.

choices.label: A write returned but the machine lost power
choices.distinguishing_question: Did the write reach a durable medium, or only the OS or device cache?
choices.why: A successful write call may establish availability in a cache without guaranteeing survival of sudden power loss.

choices.label: After reboot, a file is partially updated or missing
choices.distinguishing_question: Was the data written atomically, ordered, journaled or recoverable after a torn update?
choices.why: Protecting individual writes is different from preserving filesystem-wide invariants through a crash.

choices.label: Closing a window or disconnecting a client
choices.technical_title: Display, connection, session and process lifetime
choices.distinguishing_question: Did the application process exit, the login session end, or only its presentation transport disconnect?
choices.why: The visible client is not necessarily the owner of the running application, and remote display transport can disappear while computation continues.

choices.label: Logging out, killing a process or restarting
choices.distinguishing_question: Which state lives only in memory, which belongs to an authenticated session, and which is stored persistently?
choices.why: A session teardown may terminate processes without affecting saved files; a machine restart removes volatile state even when durable profiles remain.

navigation_bridges.question: Where is the actual trust or ownership boundary?

choices.label: An app cannot access memory or a device
choices.technical_title: Address spaces, privilege modes, mediated I/O
choices.distinguishing_question: Is access blocked by page permissions, process credentials, device driver policy or application sandbox?
choices.why: Isolation and authorization are implemented at multiple layers; kernel privilege by itself does not explain who is allowed to use a camera or file.

choices.label: A request fails across computers
choices.technical_title: Remote identity, authentication and failure boundaries
choices.distinguishing_question: Who authenticates the requester and where is the authority for the resource located?
choices.why: Local permissions do not automatically grant remote access; the other machine has its own identities, policies and failure modes.

navigation_bridges.question: Which computing experience do I actually need to own?

choices.label: I want a new interface or application environment
choices.technical_title: Kernel contract versus shell and application platform
choices.distinguishing_question: Can an existing kernel and drivers already provide the safety, storage and device services needed?
choices.why: Replacing the user experience is often possible without rewriting the kernel; the motivation determines the minimal useful system boundary.

choices.label: I need unusual timing, devices or isolation
choices.distinguishing_question: Which hardware guarantees, latency constraints and fault models cannot be satisfied by reused components?
choices.why: A single-function device may simplify process and storage requirements while making deadlines and physical recovery more stringent.

navigation_bridges.question: What actually prevents concurrent work from finishing?

choices.label: Tasks interleave and corrupt shared state
choices.distinguishing_question: Which shared invariant becomes false under a particular interleaving?
choices.why: Mutual exclusion protects a critical invariant, not arbitrary application correctness. A reproducible interleaving reveals the missing synchronization.

choices.label: Tasks wait forever or starve
choices.distinguishing_question: Is there a cycle of dependencies, repeated unproductive retry, or systematic unfairness?
choices.why: Deadlock, livelock and starvation can all look like a freeze but require different interventions.

navigation_bridges.question: Where is shared state actually located?

choices.label: Two machines share a user experience
choices.technical_title: Remote execution, identity and session transport
choices.distinguishing_question: Is the application running here or elsewhere, and what remains alive if the connection drops?
choices.why: A remote screen can look local without sharing its process, filesystem or failure domain.

choices.label: Several machines cooperate on one result
choices.distinguishing_question: How do retries, duplicated requests and inconsistent views of state affect correctness?
choices.why: A crashed remote task and a lost reply are observationally similar; retrying without idempotency can execute an operation twice.

entry_model: One question or a related question set selects a purpose-conditioned projection of canonical OS mechanisms and source locations. Candidate chapter locators remain reading leads, not proof certificates.
